learn.explain: AI models are usually priced by tokens. A token is a small piece of text, roughly three-quarters of an English word; Vietnamese often uses more tokens for the same meaning. You pay for input tokens, everything the model reads, including the instructions, the conversation history and any documents you send, and for output tokens, everything it writes, which are more expensive. So the monthly bill depends on how many requests there are, how much text goes into each one, and how long the answers are. Bills change when usage grows, when a new feature sends whole documents instead of short extracts, or when conversations get long, because the history is re-sent every time. Costs can be controlled with shorter prompts, sending only relevant text, caching repeated content, limiting answer length and using smaller models for simple tasks.
points: You pay for text read (input) and text written (output); output costs more.
Bills grow with traffic, document length and long conversations.
Controls: send less text, cache repeated parts, use cheaper models for easy tasks.
learn.analogy: Think of it like a taxi meter. You pay for distance, and the meter runs both ways: reading is like the trip there, writing is the trip back, and the trip back costs more per kilometre. A bill doubles not because the price changed, but because more trips were taken, or longer ones.

model: The AI is priced like a taxi meter: you pay per use. The unit is a token, a small piece of text, roughly three-quarters of a word. You pay for everything the AI reads, your instructions, the conversation and any documents, and everything it writes, and writing costs more. So the bill depends on three things: how many requests there are, how much text goes into each one, and how long the answers are. This month the bill almost doubled, and when I looked into it, the price didn't change at all. Two things happened. Your usage grew about thirty percent, which is good news. And the new contract-review feature sends the whole contract every time, instead of just the relevant pages. Those small amounts add up. The good news is that we can keep costs under control. First, we send only the relevant pages, which should cut that feature's cost by more than half. Second, the instructions are the same for every request, so we can reuse them at a much lower price. And for simple tasks, like sorting emails, a smaller model gives you better bang for your buck. The trade-off is quality, so we'll test each change first. Based on that, my rough estimate is that next month comes back close to the old level.
short: AI is priced per use, like a taxi meter, in small pieces of text called tokens. The bill almost doubled because usage grew thirty percent and the new contract feature sends whole contracts. We'll send only the relevant pages, reuse repeated instructions, and use a smaller model for simple tasks. My rough estimate: back near last month's level.

audience.engineer: Cost breakdown from the usage logs: requests up about thirty percent month on month, but tokens per request on the contract-review endpoint went from roughly six thousand input tokens to forty-five thousand, because we're stuffing the full contract into context. That one endpoint is now sixty percent of spend. Fixes, in order: retrieve only the relevant clauses instead of the full document; restructure the prompt so the long static system prompt and the tool definitions come first and enable prompt caching on them; cap max tokens on the summary output; and route email triage to a smaller model after checking it holds quality on the eval set. I'd also add a per-tenant cost dashboard with an alert.

followUps.q: Can you give us a fixed monthly price instead?
followUps.answer: The provider charges us per use, so a fixed price would mean either you overpay in quiet months or we take a risk in busy ones. What I can do is set a monthly budget with an alert at eighty percent, so there are never surprises.

followUps.q: Will using a cheaper model make the answers worse?
followUps.answer: For some tasks, yes, which is why we only switch where tests show the quality holds. Sorting emails into five categories is easy; drafting legal summaries is not. We'll match the model to the task.
Because the text is cut into more, smaller pieces for Vietnamese than for English, so the same message uses more units. It's usually a moderate difference, and we include it in the estimate.
